Q29385468.summary: A gilded openwork shell of fruited grapevine encloses a plain silver inner cup. Within the loops of the vine sit twelve figures holding scrolls, accompanied by birds, a lamb, a rabbit and an eagle; two of them, the most youthful, are thought to be images of Christ. Once hailed as the Holy Grail, the object is now seen as a fine 6th-century liturgical vessel, perhaps a standing lamp.
facts: When it surfaced in the early 20th century, its inner cup was claimed to be the cup of the Last Supper; it was exhibited as the Holy Grail at the 1933 Chicago World's Fair, a claim never substantiated.
The Met notes that its shape most closely resembles 6th-century standing lamps, perhaps alluding to Christ's words 'I am the light of the world'.
It has been argued to belong to a treasure of the church of Saint Sergios at Kaper Koraon, southeast of Antioch.
Q29385468.notes: Christ's presence rests on the Met's statement that two of the twelve figures 'are thought to be' Christ; they cannot be distinguished in the thumbnail. The other ten have been read as apostles or classical philosophers. Authenticity has at times been questioned.
